photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard; photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The photo documents Indigenous people on the Fraser River drying salmon on a wooden rack, a traditional Coast Salish/Fraser Canyon fishing practice; museum itself notes "Halkomelem?" (a Coast Salish-speaking group), fitting the region even if the specific group can't be confirmed from the image alone.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Documentary photograph of Coast Salish men standing before elevated timber salmon caches with fishing spears and net poles along the Fraser River, depicting traditional fishing/storage architecture and material culture of the people.

photo.name: stereoscope photograph
photo.title: stereoscope photograph (black and white)
photo.reason: The photo shows a wooden anthropomorphic house-post/guardian figure at the entrance of a Snuneymuxw (Coast Salish) longhouse in Nanaimo, a documentary image of Coast Salish architecture and carving.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white and halftone lithographic colour); photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Postcard photograph of an Indigenous man and woman at a wood-shingled plank house/outbuilding at Whonnock, BC — a Coast Salish (Halkomelem-speaking) community — documenting traditional dwelling and daily life.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Studio portrait of James Sqwameyuks, identified as a Songhees (Coast Salish) chief, wearing Western-style jacket, waistcoat and trousers; a documentary photograph of a Coast Salish individual fits the claimed ethnicity.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black and white); photographic print
photo.reason: Postcard photo of two infants in colourful woven/beaded cradleboard wraps, a traditional Coast Salish (and broader Northwest Coast) infant-carrying practice, captioned "Native Skookum Indian Papooses, British Columbia" — a genuine documentary image of dress/craft in use, despite the exoticizing tourist-postcard framing.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white and halftone lithographic colour); photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Studio postcard showing three Northwest Coast men in regalia; the museum identifies the man on the right (cloth cap with feather) as Coast Salish, making this a documentary photo of Coast Salish dress alongside neighbouring peoples.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black and white); photographic print
photo.reason: Documentary studio/postcard portrait of a Sechelt (Coast Salish) woman and child in early 20th-century dress, captioned "Sechelt Indians, British Columbia," matching the claimed Coast Salish ethnicity and photo category.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Documentary photo of two Coast Salish men poling a dugout canoe through rapids on the Cowichan River, a traditional daily-life/travel scene consistent with the claimed people and location.

household.name: comb
household.title: comb
household.reason: A double-sided wooden comb with carved concentric-circle/oval designs, a style consistent with Coast Salish woodwork; the museum notes it as a modern attribution, which is sufficient identification rather than a mere "style" caveat.

household.name: tray
household.title: tray
household.reason: A coiled cedar-root basketry tray with imbricated geometric designs, a classic Coast Salish weaving technique and form used for daily household purposes.

household.name: basket
household.title: basket
household.reason: A coiled cedar-bark basket with imbricated geometric designs, a classic Coast Salish weaving technique and form, matching the claimed attribution.

household.name: öskar
household.title: öskar
household.reason: The object is a cedar-bark bailer used to remove water from canoes, a type of household water-management tool attributed by Hilary Stewart to the Coast Salish, matching British Columbia provenance.

household.name: cradle; head-flattener
household.title: cradle; head-flattener
household.reason: A wooden model cradle with woven lacing and padding, made by Coast Salish people to demonstrate traditional infant head-flattening practice — a genuine ethnographic household object of this culture.

household.name: basket
household.title: basket
household.reason: A coiled cedar-root basket with imbricated geometric designs, a classic Coast Salish weaving technique and form, matching the claimed ethnicity and attributed maker.

household.name: basket
household.title: basket
household.reason: A rectangular woven cedar-root/splint basket tray with coiled construction, a well-known Coast Salish basketry form and technique, matching the museum's attribution.

household.name: korg, basket
household.title: korg, basket
household.reason: A woven cedar bark fiber basket with decorative banding, collected in Canada and consistent with Northwest Coast basketry traditions including Coast Salish work; the museum's own comparative reference (Hilary Stewart's "Cedar") supports this attribution.

jewelry.name: bracelet
jewelry.title: bracelet
jewelry.reason: A mountain goat horn bracelet with incised line and circle decoration is a well-worn personal ornament of a type made on the Northwest Coast; the label only says "North West Coast of America," not specifically Coast Salish, but the object is plausible for the region and Coast Salish cannot be ruled out from neighbouring groups' work.

architectural.name: drawing
architectural.title: drawing
architectural.reason: This is an 1859 watercolour by a European settler artist depicting a Coast Salish grave structure near Victoria, documenting the people's burial practice/architecture; it is outsider artwork about the culture but the subject matter (a Coast Salish grave box) is genuine ethnographic evidence, made by the people even if drawn by an outsider — the object depicted belongs, though the artwork itself is not Coast Salish-made.
